subtitle: A draft contents list for a planned binder of the main Internet protocol documents.

tldr.problem: The Internet family of protocols was replacing the old ARPANET protocols, and people needed one place to find the documents that defined them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the draft table of contents of an Internet Protocol Handbook, grouped into Overview, Gateway Level, Host Level, Application Level and Appendices, with the RFC or IEN number for each entry.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the earlier draft list in RFC 766 and is only a contents list, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 774 replaces the earlier draft contents list in RFC 766. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown, and the memo itself is a draft contents list, not a specification.

sections.title: The Planned Handbook
sections.content:
RFC 774 says the internet family of protocols was replacing the old ARPANET protocols. To support that, the Network Information Center was to prepare an Internet Protocol Handbook, tentatively planned to be available at the end of 1980.

The Handbook would closely parallel the old ARPANET Protocol Handbook and would mostly be a collection of existing RFCs and IENs. Suggestions for additions were to be sent to Jon Postel.
sections.eli5: Before the internet rules were scattered everywhere, someone planned to gather the important ones into one binder.

sections.title: How the Contents Are Organized
sections.content:
The draft table of contents has five groups. Overview holds the catenet model for internetworking (IEN-48). Gateway Level starts with the Internet Protocol (IEN-128, RFC 760) and also lists gateway routing, building a gateway, gateway monitoring and performance measurement message formats.

Host Level lists the User Datagram Protocol (RFC 768), the Transmission Control Protocol (IEN-129, RFC 761) and the Multiplexing Protocol (IEN-90). Application Level covers the time server, name server and trivial file transfer protocols, Telnet, File Transfer Protocol, Mail Transfer Protocol and the Internet Message Protocol.

The Appendices list Assigned Numbers (RFC 770), Address Mappings (IEN-115), Document File Format Standards (RFC 678) and Mail Header Format Standards (RFC 733).
sections.eli5: The binder is sorted like a building: big picture first, then the parts that move packets between networks, then the parts computers use to talk, then the programs people use, then reference tables at the back.

sections.title: Finding the Documents
sections.content:
The memo notes that RFCs and IENs are public access files that can be copied from the Network Information Center online Library at SRI-KL using FTP with the user name ANONYMOUS and password GUEST.

IEN pathnames look like <NETINFO>IEN-nnn.TXT and RFC pathnames look like <NETINFO>RFCnnn.TXT, where nnn is the document number. The memo points out an inconsistency: IENs have a hyphen in the pathname and RFCs do not.
sections.eli5: The memo also tells you where to download each paper and warns that two kinds of file names are spelled slightly differently.
